summary:
Texas restricts trans people's use of sex-separated facilities under the Women's Privacy Act, signed by Governor Greg Abbott on 22 September 2025 and effective 4 December 2025. The law requires restrooms to match the sex recorded on a person's birth certificate and applies to public schools, universities, prisons and Texas government buildings. Facilities face a $25,000 fine for a first violation and $125,000 for subsequent violations. The gender-placements statute reaches prisons only as to restroom use; it does not govern cell assignment or the housing placement of trans prisoners.

Enforcement began immediately. On 6 December 2025 Department of Public Safety troopers checked identification at women's restrooms outside the Capitol; trans women holding female identity markers were admitted. The Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and opponents warned that unclear guidelines produce uneven and invasive enforcement. Protests followed at the Capitol.

In April 2026 Attorney General Ken Paxton's second complaint escalated the state's probe of the Austin Independent School District over its bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint. It is the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry directed at a school district.

An independent legal-risk assessment places Texas in its top "Do Not Travel" tier for adult trans travellers, one of four states so graded alongside Florida, Idaho and Kansas, scored law-by-law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture.

House Bill 229, the Women's Bill of Rights, passed in May 2025, was signed in June 2025 and took effect in September 2025. It defines female as a person who can biologically produce ova and male as one who can biologically fertilise ova, requires people with disorders of sex development to select one binary gender with no third-gender recognition, applies across all state statutes, regulations and laws using gendered terms, and bans any change of sex on Texas driver's licences and birth certificates. Before that change, altering a birth certificate's gender indicator required a court order, with judicial discretion often referencing WPATH Standards of Care, a narrative statement from a doctor or therapist that care was appropriate and the change in the person's best interest, and no specific treatment requirement including surgery. On 30 January 2025 Governor Abbott separately directed state agencies to recognise only two genders.

Texas's hate-crime statute enhances penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, and it is rarely prosecuted. No state law bars employment, housing, public-accommodations or insurance discrimination based on gender identity. Texas courts recognised federal employment protections under Bostock v. Clayton County in March 2021. Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio prohibit gender-identity discrimination in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations; Denton, El Paso, Arlington, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Irving, Lubbock, Mesquite and Waco have narrower city-employment or public-accommodation protections.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by Lawrence v. Texas in June 2003, but Texas remains one of three states retaining a dormant same-sex-only sodomy law, termed deviate sexual intercourse; a 2025 repeal passed by the House failed in the Senate. The state's Romeo-and-Juliet affirmative defence is available only where the actor is not more than three years older than a child under 17 or is the child's spouse and not of the child's same sex, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship does not have the same statutory defence.

Marriage licensing in Texas was restricted to a man and a woman by House Bill 103 of 1973, effective 1 January 1974, followed by a 1997 licensing ban, 2003 non-recognition of marriages and civil unions, and a 2005 constitutional referendum; federal and state rulings struck the ban in 2014, and Obergefell v. Hodges legalised same-sex marriage nationwide on 26 June 2015, with about 2,500 licences issued within months. Texas does not recognise domestic partnerships statewide. Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, El Paso, Houston and San Antonio provide health insurance to domestic partners of city workers; Dallas County paid $300 per month cash subsidies from October 2012; Travis, El Paso and Bexar Counties allow partner participation; and Pflugerville ISD allows inclusion at full worker cost. Houston's 2001 Proposition 2 barred city domestic-partner benefits except for legal spouses, later interpreted in November 2013 to require spousal benefits for legally married same-sex couples, and an April 2013 Attorney General opinion held the state constitution bars political-subdivision benefits based on domestic-partnership status as similar to marriage.

House Bill 643, prefiled in November 2022, would expand the definition of sexually oriented business to restrict any performance in which a performer uses clothing, makeup or other markers to exhibit a gender variance from birth-assigned sex while singing, lip-syncing, dancing or otherwise performing. It would capture transgender performers in any role and cisgender portrayals of diverse or ambiguous genders, and would criminalise minors' attendance at drag shows.
tangentialFactors:
Texas is one of three states retaining a dormant same-sex-only sodomy law; Kansas struck a similar statute in 2005, and Texas repeal bills died in 2013. A 2025 repeal passed the House but failed in the Senate.

Enforcement of the facilities law is contested between levels of government. The Austin City Council moved to circumvent the statute's intent while the attorney general's office escalated a records demand against a school district, so where a trans visitor encounters the law depends on the locality and the institution.

Religious-refusal provisions shape service access. Senate Bill 1978, enacted in June 2019, bars adverse government action against people or organisations supporting religious bodies that may refuse LGBTQ service, and judges who refuse to officiate same-sex weddings on religious grounds face no punishment as of 2025.

Other measures in force or under challenge include a September 2025 law listing banned diversity, equity and inclusion school and certain workplace programmes for sexual orientation, which is under court challenge, and a constitutional parental-rights amendment passed by voters in November 2025.

Roughly fifty bills filed in early January 2023 sought to criminalise youth gender-affirming care, reduce adult access, bar sex-marker changes for minors and further restrict sports participation by transgender or gender-nonconforming people.
localsOnly:
Senate Bill 14, signed in June 2023, effectively bans gender-affirming care for minors. It followed a February 2022 Attorney General opinion classifying such care as child abuse and Governor Abbott's directives ordering the Department of Family and Protective Services to investigate parents who facilitate it, with criminal penalties for knowing failure to report. Five district attorneys refused to follow the directive, and a March 2022 temporary injunction was reinstated by the Third Court of Appeals after a suit by the ACLU and Lambda Legal on behalf of providers including Dr. Megan Mooney and a family with a 16-year-old transgender girl on puberty blockers. An investigative supervisor testified that trans-child cases faced different rules, with mandatory investigation regardless of evidence and a prohibition on discussing cases by email or text.

The June 2025 Parents' Bill of Rights bars school employees from teaching or discussing gender identity, bans LGBT-related student organisations, mandates deadnaming and misgendering of trans students, and expands parental authority.

In Gibson v. Collier, Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman incarcerated by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice and diagnosed with gender dysphoria, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the department's official treatment policy excluded it. The federal district court denied the state's immunity defences but ruled against her on the Eighth Amendment claim; the Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding no deliberate indifference and holding that refusing surgery is a permissible medical choice under Kosilek, with Judge Barksdale dissenting on summary-judgement procedure.

Any adult may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, and legally married same-sex couples may adopt jointly and obtain supplemental birth certificates listing both parents. Lesbian couples may access IVF and assisted insemination, though health-plan IVF coverage that requires fertilisation only with the spouse's sperm restricts access. Federally funded adoption agencies may discriminate on religious grounds.

An October 2020 internal policy permits social workers to discriminate against LGBT clients, and in February 2022 The Trevor Project was removed from state suicide-prevention resources.
outOfScopeNotes:
The operative status of several measures is unresolved. House Bill 643 was prefiled in November 2022 and its enactment status is not sourced here. The September 2025 diversity, equity and inclusion law is under court challenge. The 2025 repeal of the dormant sodomy law passed the House and failed in the Senate, leaving the statute on the books.

The scope of the facilities law's prison provisions is limited to restroom use; whether cell assignment or housing placement will be addressed by further legislation is not sourced.

Enforcement guidelines for the facilities law are described by opponents as unclear, and the resulting uneven enforcement is documented rather than measured. The legal-risk tiering that places Texas among four "Do Not Travel" states rests on a five-year legislation-tracking methodology whose scoring detail is not reproduced here.

Whether the attorney general's probe of the Austin Independent School District will produce a formal enforcement action is unresolved.
